| IV | **The construction of the porch's proportion, drawn on the ground** | inscription | ○ unbuilt | Dallington 1592 p. 55 | Poliphilo works out the architect's rule by drawing it: he takes a square off the two columns either side, makes a tetragon ABCD, divides it with three lines each way into sixteen quadrats, adds half as much again to get twenty-four, draws the two diagonals and two more lines to make four quadrats mutually intersecting, then sets four median points in the void over the isopleures and joins them into a rhombus. This is the book being a treatise for a page, and it is the reason the porch is described at all. Nothing in the world shows it; grepping for tetragon, rhombus and quadrat finds only unrelated canvas code. |
| IV | **What the architect must be, and the rule of the solid** | inscription | ○ unbuilt | Dallington 1592 pp. 56-57 | The digression the proportion figure sets off. Then the architect himself: honest, no prattler, courteous, patient, full of new devices, a curious searcher into all arts, and not subject to avarice. Belongs in the commentary layer rather than in geometry, but it is one of the few places the book states its own method, and the world does not carry it anywhere. |

| XXV | **The whole family metamorphosed into the rivers and founts of Treviso: the father into the river Sile, the mother into the fountain Calardia, siblings into rivulets, a kingfisher (Alcyoneo) and a water-strider (Tipula)** | place | ○ unbuilt | our translation (CC0), translation/en/page_384.md (p. 384) | The chapter's most systematic Ovidian aetiology: Murgania, Quintia, Septimia become wells/founts; Alimbrica is made ash then a little river; Astorgia and Melmia become little rivers running into their father; the father Lelio Siliro himself becomes the river Sile (Treviso's real river, from his 'truncated name'); the mother Calardia becomes the fountain Calardia; the second son Musilistre becomes a rivulet 'inundating the Altinate peoples'; the two youngest sons are transformed into a kingfisher (Alcyoneo, 'clad with regal and incorruptible plumes') and a water-strider (Tipula). The land around Treviso literally IS Polia's punished family -- this is the single richest, most buildable piece of new geography the chapter offers (a river-god figure for the Sile, a fountain for Calardia, a kingfisher and a water-strider as attendant creatures) and nothing in the world reflects it. |

| XXVI | **Polia measures her own cruelty against Daphne, Medea, Atreus and Thyestes, Theseus, Narcissus, and above all Anaxarete -- who was turned to stone for letting Iphis die of love** | picture | ○ unbuilt | p. 396 | 'Harder than Daphne. More wicked than Medea. More iniquitous than Atreus and Thyestes. More dire than Theseus. More fugitive than Narcissus. Much more harsh than Anaxarete to her cruel Iphis.' Anaxarete is the GOVERNING exemplum: Ovid's cruel maiden who let Iphis hang himself for her and was petrified by Venus in punishment (Met. XIV) -- the precise myth of a beloved punished for a lover's love-death, and Polia's clearest self-prophecy (Book II's coming punishment-vision and conversion answer exactly this). Nothing in the world names or depicts Anaxarete anywhere; a statue of a woman mid-transformation to stone, sited at or near the temple, would be the single most legible piece of foreshadowing Book II could have and currently has none. Strong candidate for the chapter's most distinctive unbuilt feature. |

| XXXII | **The chapter's catalogue of classical exempla: Bellerophon, Polycrates, Battus, Siccius Dentatus's front-facing scars, Perillus's bronze bull, Herostratus, Laodamia/Protesilaus, Ariadne on Naxos, Io** | inscription | ○ unbuilt | pp. 436, 437, 441, 442, 443 | Poliphilo argues almost entirely by classical exemplum: perseverance (Bellerophon, Polycrates and the touchstone, p. 436), honourable endurance (Siccius Dentatus's wounds all in front, p. 437), his burning torment (Perillus roasted in his own bronze bull, p. 442), his self-reproach at cursing Polia (Herostratus burning Diana's temple at Ephesus, p. 443), and his grief at her leaving the festival (Laodamia weeping for Protesilaus, Ariadne abandoned on Naxos, Io transformed, p. 441). Venus legally binds Cupid to complete the union he started, on the mother's own authority -- a striking, specific legal-mythic image (the god of love as a bonded defendant) that nothing in the world currently depicts. | XXXV | **The soul returns bearing Polia's name sealed within, not carved and fading like Oenone and Paris's names in the bark** | relief | ○ unbuilt | our translation (CC0), translation/en/page_460.md (p. 460) | 'That most-celebrated name, in me impressed, by which, from thee, I receded; which, otherwise, is carved and impressed, and sealed, within me, vegetable and fecund -- (it) was not that of Oenone and of Paris, sculpted in the ramose trees and rugose barks, nor thence ever shall it be erased.' Invokes the Oenone/Paris myth of names carved in tree-bark that fade as an explicit FOIL to Poliphilo's permanent, soul-sealed devotion. A tree bearing faded/half-erased 'OENONE' and 'PARIS' carvings, sited as an ironic counter-monument, would pair naturally with xxxiv-myrrha-tears (Myrrha's weeping bark) as a small pair of unhappy-love trees in the Book II precinct -- two mythological trees, neither built. |

Come, my heart, domicile of irritable ardour. Come, extreme part where makes residence my exhorter Cupid -- and let us make, then, the festive Soteria (thanksgivings) for thy retrograde reformation (return).' A named thanksgiving rite -- Soteria, 'a saving' -- for the soul's safe return, distinct from and following the throne-vision. The book gives no liturgical detail beyond the name and the occasion, so any build would be generic (garlands, an offering) rather than textually specific; recorded here rather than declined because the rite is named and its occasion is exact, unlike the truly undescribed Polyandrion medallions. |

PARTIAL, and for a siting reason like chapter XI's torch-nymph: the world already stages a priestess with kissing lovers before her -- src/scenes/world/tombs.js _buildBookTwo's 'Venus-priestess enthroned' group (labelled in its own code comment 'ENTHRONED . The classical Ovidian gold/lead arrow pair (Metamorphoses I: gold kindles love, lead repels it), here turned from the lovers' own torment into a standing curse that PROTECTS their union. Grepped src/data/tours.json and src/data/hp_dream.js: Cupid's golden arrow appears twice elsewhere in the built world (the fountain-unveiling at the theatre of Venus, ch. XI/XXXV-adjacent, and the vision at Venus's throne, ch. A landscape passage (many-coloured meadows, fruit-groves) the dream walk does not currently traverse at this point in the story, ending with the nymphs' final exit and the lovers left alone -- the hinge into the book's last scene. |

Every label the world gives Polia elsewhere is plain 'Polia'. |

Polia answers, 'Poliphilo, my delight, my sole festive refrigerium ... licentious dominator of my sworded and transfixed little heart -- to --' and the chapter division cuts her off. tours.json's 'book_two' lede summarises the avowals generally ('They make their final avowals') but none of this page's specific imagery -- Philoctetes, the Terebinth of Hebron, the diamantine chains -- appears anywhere in the corpus of built text. |
| XXXVIII | **Poliphilo wishes the Sun had granted him the long night of Alcmena, or the Stygian sleep out of Psyche's box** | inscription | ◐ partial | p. 465 | 'he who would not endure (because, I judge, with a goddess it is not permitted) to grant me the long night of Alcmena. Ah me, why did he not exchange a little of his swiftness for a little sloth ... And why was the Stygian sleep out of curious Psyche's box not laid upon me then?' Two paired classical allusions -- Jupiter doubling the night to beget Hercules on Alcmena, and the drugged sleep from Pandora's-box-like device in Apuleius. Grepped src/data/hp_dream.js and tours.json: the Psyche's-box half is quoted almost verbatim in hp_dream.js's 'awakening' stop ('Why was he not given the drugged sleep out of Psyche's box?'), but 'Alcmena' does not occur anywhere in either file -- the paired allusion is cut in half. The dropped half is the one that most directly compares Poliphilo's loss to a god's stolen night with a mortal woman. |
| XXXVIII | **Philomela (the nightingale), hidden in the brambles before daybreak, singing out Tereus's rape** | creature | ◐ partial | p. 465 | 'And there Philomela, weeping before daybreak, hidden among thorny brambles and in thickets close with the dark foliage of small oaks wound about with twining honeysuckle, was pouring out the violence of that adulterous and faithless Tereus, saying with tuneful chatter: Tereus, Tereus -- [?have I been wronged].' The page's own note flags the Greek (eme ebiasato, 'he forced/violated me') as corrupt and unverified against the facsimile. Grepped src/data/tours.json: the 'wood' waking stop names her generically -- 'He wakes to the nightingale -- Philomela, the bird of lament and of dawn -- the classical sign that the night of vision is over' -- but stops there. Grepped src/data/hp_dream.js: she is reduced further, to an unnamed 'nightingale ... singing in the thorns before daybreak'. Nowhere in the built world is Tereus named, the rape stated, the specific setting (brambles, small-oak thickets, honeysuckle) given, or the bird's own cry ('Tereus, Tereus') quoted. This is the most specific classical allusion on the book's last page and the least built of the four features here -- arguably the single most interesting thing this chapter has that the world does not (see report). |

### Chapter XI  · Book 1 · 1499 pp. 141–146

*Research: **enumerated**. Chapter XI has NO PLATE of its own and, until this pass, no feature list -- and it looked covered, which is why it stayed unread. The reason it looked covered is a mistake in tours.json: the Human Chess Match and Logistica and Thelemia were both tagged chapter XI, so this chapter's row showed two tour stops. Both are chapter X. The chess ballet is at 1499 p. 119 -- "Through the way of the curtains there entered thirty-two young girls, of whom sixteen were clothed in cloth of gold" -- and page_119.md's own heading says Chapter X. Retagged in this pass; ticket bug-chapter-xi-tour-misattributed has the consequences.

What the chapter actually contains is one of the hinges of Book I: the bath nymphs leave Poliphilo alone and kindled on a plain, he walks to the end of a flowery covering, an ample plain opens with a countless crowd of youth of BOTH KINDS keeping high festival, and out of that company a nymph comes to him with a BURNING TORCH in her hand. He suspects she is Polia and the strange dress and place talk him out of it. Then five pages of blazon -- gown, girdle, pearls, necklace stone by stone, wreath, hair, eyes -- and a closing quarrel between his eyes and his appetite.

Eleven features. The one that matters is xi-nymph-with-the-torch, and it is PARTIAL for an interesting reason: the world already builds a Polia holding a burning torch, and constants.js already describes her pose as "in the green arbour, before he has recognised her" -- which is this chapter's moment, word for word. She is simply sited three chapters later, in the jasmine arbour, with no festival behind her.*

### Chapter XII  · Book 1 · 1499 pp. 147–152

*Research: **enumerated**. The chapter has no explicit rubric in the Dallington markdown, so its boundaries were located by content-matching unique phrases against translation/en, which DOES carry '# Page NNN — Chapter XII' headers for every page even though our translation is only the pipeline's assigned source for chapters XVII+. Chapter XII runs Dallington pp. [204]-214 (the argument 'The most fayre Nymph beeing come to Poliphilus, bearing a Torch...' opens it right after chapter XI's Bibria-laurel line on p. 204/205, and it closes with '...bridling my inconuenient desires' on p. 214, immediately before chapter XIII's own argument 'Polia, as yet vnknowne to her Louer Poliphilus...'). That is 1499 pp. 147-152, matching the ledger's derived range exactly.

The WHOLE chapter, read in full, is a single unbroken scene: the beautiful torch-bearing nymph (introduced in chapter XI, still unrecognised) comes up to Poliphilo, takes his hand, and leads him walking; he is overwhelmed, half-believes she is Polia, nearly declares himself, checks himself with a flood of classical exempla about presumption and unfulfillable desire, and ends still resolved to love her in silence. There is no architecture, garden or building described anywhere in these six pages -- it is pure interior monologue and rhetorical simile, continuing chapter XI's blazon and setting up chapter XIII's recognition crisis.

TWO DATA-QUALITY FINDINGS worth flagging for whoever next touches the neighbouring chapters (I did not edit either file; only coverage.json is mine to write):
  (1) src/data/poliphilo.json tags two utterances 'chapter: XIII' that are actually inside chapter XII by the boundary above: the apostrophe sourced 'Dallington p. 207' ('Oh happie hee that may enioy...') and the speech sourced 'Dallington p. 212' ('Oh delycate and heauenly Damosell...'). Both are read on the running page's default-on 'Poliphilo speaking' lens (main.js, station 'polia') -- the content is very likely live, but under the wrong chapter tag. Not fixed here; that file is not coverage.json.
  (2) hp.db.page_concordance's own section column flips from JOURNEY_DOORS to PROCESSION exactly at 1499 p. 149 -- i.e. at the same page the printed woodcuts (catalog #44 on) begin -- even though the PROCESSION text itself (the triumphal-car reliefs) is not actually narrated until chapter XIII/XIV. The corpus's own section tags follow the images, not the prose; a second, independent confirmation of 'the plates are an index, not an inventory' cutting the other way -- here the index runs AHEAD of the text, not silently past it.

Plates: the ledger's derived plates 44-49 (page_seq 149-152) are the Triumph-of-Europa car and its first reliefs, and the start of Leda's reliefs -- confirmed by eye against hp1499_p149.jpg (PRIMA TABELLA / SECVNDA SINISTRA panels) and hp1499_p152.jpg (the TRIVMPHVS full-page car, one leaf off from the catalogue's own page_seq=151, a common facsimile/catalogue offset). None of this is DESCRIBED in chapter XII's own text -- Poliphilo does not reach the triumphs until the chapter XIII/XIV argument 'drawing near to the triumphs, he saw countless young men and girls keeping festival' -- but the woodcuts are physically printed on these leaves, so they are listed below as this chapter's plates per the recipe, with the mismatch noted on each. All six are already modelled in the world (Triumphs._buildTriumphs, src/scenes/world/triumphs.js; TRIUMPH_RELIEFS.europa/.leda, src/scenes/world/constants.js) -- grep evidence only, not verified live this session.

Measurements: chapter XII states no size, distance or count anywhere. The only quantifiable/orientational detail in six pages is a single handedness: the nymph carries her torch in her LEFT hand and takes Poliphilo's hand with the other. Recorded below as the one measurement entry; everything else in the chapter is simile.*

| ✅ | The three doors hewn in the living rock<br>*Built and verified on the running page 2026-09-09 at main.js?v=361, standing at the station (0, 21) looking north to the gates at z = 12.

The note this replaces described a build that no longer exists: "a free-standing 29 m masonry wall on a garden axis, the wrong ground, the wrong material and the wrong mood". The wall with its entablature and Corinthian columns — the opposite of "as plaine as might be" — had already been replaced by rock: a bank of boulders rising behind and above the gates, a straight-cut rock face with the three openings hewn from it, rough reveals, and the green moss the book gives the right-hand gate's leaves. So the material and the mood were right and the ledger had simply not been told.

What was still wrong was the GROUND, which is the third of the three faults and the one the book is most insistent about: "without any greene grasse or hearbe". The meadow was excluded from a strip only 2.8 m deep at the foot of the rock, so grass grew over the whole approach a reader actually crosses, and the stony ground stopped short of it. Now the exclusion covers the seat (x -15.5..15.5, z 5.5..19.5), the stone apron runs back to z = 19 to meet it, and 54 broken stones are strewn across it for "full of broken and nybled stones" — small, flat and un-collided, since the book's complaint is that the place is harsh underfoot, not that it is hard to cross.

Cost, measured: 5 621 -> 5 625 meshes and 3 101 652 -> 3 103 586 triangles. The 54 stones merge to about four draws because they share a material.

Still short of the book in one respect, recorded rather than hidden: the crags rise "as high as a man might looke to" and ours are a bank of boulders a few metres tall. The mountains behind are not built.* | building | `world/portal.js _buildDoorsWall; the meadow exclusion in world/nature.js` | Dallington p. 192 |

### Chapter XIV  · Book 1 · 1499 pp. 158–176

*Research: **enumerated**. All 19 pages read in full (pp. 158-176: the festival crowd around the four triumphal cars; Triumph 1, Europa on the bull, drawn by six centaurs, emerald-and-diamond car, four reliefs including the NEMO panel; Triumph 2, Leda and the swan on cloth-of-gold cushions, drawn by six white elephants, agate-and-sapphire car, four reliefs including Cupid painting the zodiac; Triumph 3, Danae on a six-cornered green jasper seat gazing at gold in her lap, drawn by six unicorns, chrysolite-and-heliotrope car, four reliefs; Triumph 4, no rider at all -- instead a gold base on four eagles carrying a jacinth urn full of holy ash (Semele's), with two carved relief bands (Jove and the seven nymphs turning into trees; a serpent-crowned god's vine-harvest), four gemstone candelabra with undying flames, and a golden vine canopy, drawn by six spotted tigers of Hyrcania, asbestos-and-carbuncle car; then the Bacchic rout -- Maenads, Silenus on his ass, a sacrificial goat, a wicker-fan bearer, and the named retinue of Mimallones, satyrs, bacchantes, Lenae, Thyiads, Naiads, Tityri and Nymphs. Checked src/scenes/world/triumphs.js (_buildTriumphs, _triumphCar, _triumphBeast, _harness, _riderInstrument, _reliefScene, _reliefTexture) and src/scenes/world/constants.js (TRIUMPHS, TRIUMPH_LIVERY, TRIUMPH_RELIEFS) by grep for every named object and creature (eagle, jasper, jacinth, ash urn, candelabra, Semele, Danae, Hyrcania, tiger, leopard, Maenad, Silenus, thyrsus, Bacchant, Mimallon, goat, wicker fan). Finding: the world already runs a real, well-researched version of the FOUR TRIUMPHAL CARS (europa/leda/danae/bacchus keys in TRIUMPHS match this chapter's four loves of Jove exactly, and PROCESSIONS.md documents two real corrections against the plates -- unicorns not horses for Danae, and the fourth car renamed from a nonexistent 'Triumph of Semele' to 'Festival of Bacchus'). But three structural things the chapter states are still wrong or missing everywhere: (1) each car's LIVERY is supposed to differ -- Europa's blue/crimson/green is not Leda's crimson/yellow/violet, and Danae's is uniform with no rank at all -- but one flat array (TRIUMPH_LIVERY) is applied to every car; (2) two of the four cars (Leda, Danae) have NO rider figure built at all, only the swan/tower prop, confirmed by reading the motif branches in _buildTriumphs; (3) the fourth car's team description in the book has no rider sentence at all -- the ash-urn IS its passenger -- yet the built world puts six nymph riders on it same as the others. The single biggest gap is the fourth car's own centrepiece: the detailed, measured jacinth urn of Semele's ashes on its four eagles, its two carved relief bands, the four gemstone candelabra and the golden vine canopy are all entirely absent, and none of the standing briefs (PROCESSIONS.md, VEHICLES.md) mention them -- the fourth car has always been read as 'the Bacchus car' by its team and its reliefs, never by what is actually riding on it. Also flagged: woodcuts #66-70 (Vertumnus and Pomona; the Four Seasons), which the coverage ledger's page-range derivation assigns to chapter XIV because they print on 1499 pp. 166-167 (inside this chapter's page range), do NOT appear anywhere in this chapter's text -- I read all of it and neither Vertumnus nor Pomona nor the Seasons are mentioned. tours.json itself already tags that station 'chapter XV', and the world's fifth, on-foot procession (team:'satyr', onFoot:true, key 'vertumnus') belongs there, not here -- the same page-range-vs-text-boundary mismatch chapter XI's enumeration flagged for its own tour stops.*

### Chapter XV  · Book 1 · 1499 pp. 177–180

*Research: **enumerated**. Read Dallington 1592 (corpus md/Hypnerotomachia_by_Francesco_Colonna.md) end to end across the whole plausible span of this chapter, lines ~10259-11127 (the file's own <!-- Page 241 --> through <!-- Page 260 --> HTML page-markers, which is the numbering this ledger's existing 'Dallington pp. N' citations already use -- confirmed by cross-checking known citations, e.g. chapter V's 'vaults-maze' at 'Dallington pp. 82-84' lands exactly on the vaults scene at marker 82). No woodcuts fall inside coverage.json's own pages_1499=[177,180] window (nearest plates are #70 at 1499 p.167 and #71 at p.185) -- confirmed, this chapter is plate-free as billed.

IMPORTANT BOUNDARY PROBLEM, flagged rather than silently resolved: coverage.json's pages_1499=[177,180] disagrees with this project's own tours.json, which tags the 'Vertumnus and Pomona' stop (the triumph, its rustic company, and the Four Seasons altar -- woodcuts #66 and #67-70, at 1499 folios 166-167) as chapter XV. Folios 166-167 fall inside coverage.json's own range for chapter XIV ([158,176]), not XV. I read the WIDER span anyway (from the close of the four-Jupiter-triumphs sequence through Dallington's literal FINIS) and enumerate everything in it, because: (a) the existing tour_stops entry on this very ledger record already carries 'Vertumnus and Pomona' under XV, so an XV entry with nothing for it would contradict the ledger's own derived field; (b) 'err toward including'; (c) whoever reconciles XIV/XV boundaries needs the full inventory in one place, not split by a guess. Features 1-6 below are the material that may actually belong to XIV -- flagged per-feature. Features 7-8 (the seaside temple and the blazon of the Nymph/Polia) are the only content that unambiguously falls after 1499 p.176 and before Dallington's stopping point, so THOSE are chapter XV under any reading.

SECOND FINDING, larger than mine to fix: tours.json's 'priapus' stop (chapter XVI) states as established fact that 'on facsimile page 193, in the middle of a sentence, at the word Mustulento, Robert Dallington's 1592 English stops.' It does not. I read past 'Mustulento Autumno S.' (the Autumn altar-panel's own dedication -- the word is not a fragment, it is the end of a complete Latin tag) and the corpus md file continues for roughly 200 more lines: the Winter altar-panel, the walk to an old ruined temple by the sea, and an extended blazon of the Nymph's body and dress, ending in an explicit 'FINIS.' at real printed-book page 100 (recto-only numbering; the facsimile's own collation note reads 'A-Z4, Aa-Cc4', and the signature marks I actually saw in sequence -- Y2, Z, Bb, Bb2, Cc, Cc2 -- confirm the text runs to the last gathering, not stopping mid-Z). This is the same Bodleian facsimile (STC 5577) SOURCES.md and tours.json cite for the 'stops at p.193' claim, so either that claim is simply wrong, or it describes a different, incomplete exemplar than the one this corpus's md file was OCR'd from. I have not resolved which; I flag it because it means real, usable, non-Godwin Dallington English exists for the seaside-temple scene and the blazon of Polia (features 7-8), and probably bears on how chapter XVI's researcher should scope their own read -- 'Mustulento' is not where the trail goes cold.

Measurements: one true physical dimension in the whole chapter (the hedge height), logged below. Several bare counts appear (four satyrs draw the car, three matrons govern the virgins, four altar panels) but none converts to a distance, so per the instructions only the hedge is logged as a measurement.*

### Chapter XVI  · Book 1 · 1499 pp. 181–188

*Research: **enumerated**. IMPORTANT DATA-QUALITY FINDING, read before using this chapter's features. The ledger's own pages_1499 [181,188] for chapter XVI ARE the correct 1499 Aldine folio range -- confirmed against translation/en/page_181.md..page_188.md, each of which headers itself '# Page NNN -- Chapter XVI' and page_189.md onward headers 'Chapter XVII'. BUT the text_source.file (the Dallington md, whose internal <!-- Page 181 --> .. <!-- Page 188 --> OCR markers are Dallington's OWN pagination, not the 1499's, per the note already on the record) does NOT contain chapter XVI's content at those marker numbers. Dallington's abridgement compresses roughly 60% of the book out, so by the time his own page-count reaches '181-188' he is only as far as real Colonna chapter ~XIII-XIV material (the ivied hundred-arch garden and the trigonal black-stone Trinity altar with the three golden sphinxes and the O-Omega-N obelisk -- DIMENSIONS.md already tables this same passage under 'chapters VII-XIV', citing the identical Dallington pp. 181-186). That passage IS already built (palace.js _buildPoliaArcade, and the trigonal altar/sphinx cube around palace.js:2305-2380), so nothing is lost -- it is simply mis-filed if attributed to XVI. This is the same class of bug closed by ticket bug-chapter-xi-tour-misattributed (2026-09-09, tours.json chess-match/Logistica-Thelemia mistagging) one seam further into the book, and it likely affects XIV/XV's own page ranges too since their content (a huge processional catalogue of ancient poets' mistresses, ch. XV, and Vertumnus/Pomona/the altar of the seasons, actually ch. XVII per translation/en/page_189's own argument-summary) doesn't obviously match Dallington OCR pp. 158-180 either -- a full re-audit of XIV-XVII's Dallington page assignments against the translation/en chapter headers is recommended before the next research pass on those chapters. I have used translation/en/page_181.md-page_188.md (CC0, correctly chapter-headed) as the authoritative source for THIS chapter's features, not the Dallington md's mislabeled OCR range, and read all eight pages in full plus the surrounding pages (180 and 189) for boundary context. Second finding: the tour_stops entry for chapter XVI, station 'priapus' ('The Altar of the Seasons -- where the English breaks off'), claims Dallington's English 'stops... in the middle of a sentence, at the word Mustulento' on 'facsimile page 193'. I read the complete Dallington Gutenberg text (Project Gutenberg EBook #18459, the full 1592 translation, corpus file md/Hypnerotomachia_by_Francesco_Colonna.md) straight through past that point: 'Mustulento Autumno S.' is only the Latin tag under the Autumn face of a four-sided altar (Spring/Summer/Autumn/Winter), and the English does NOT break off there -- it continues for some 700 more lines (through the Winter face, and Poliphilo and the Nymph sitting before 'an olde decaied temple') and then concludes cleanly with a resolved, complete sentence about the phoenix renewed by the sun, followed by the word 'FINIS.' printed outright, then the transcriber's own technical notes confirming 'the 1592 English translation covers just under half the Italian text.' There is no mid-sentence cutoff anywhere in this text. The general claim that Dallington's coverage ends around the threshold of the Temple of Venus (i.e., approximately where our CC0 translation's chapter XVII picks up) is directionally right and matches the transcriber's note almost exactly -- only the dramatic specifics ('mid-sentence', 'at the word Mustulento') are not supported by the corpus text and should be corrected or re-sourced. Plate #71 ('Worship of Priapus', woodcut_catalog.page_seq 185) is catalogued inside chapter XVI's folio range by the automatic page-range derivation, but the actual descriptive text of the Priapus rite is at 1499 folio 194, which translation/en/page_194.md itself headers as Chapter XVII -- so the plate's page_seq (185) is very likely keyed to where the woodcut is physically printed in the 1499 (a leaf or two ahead of its subject, common in this book), not to where the rite is described. I have kept a feature entry under XVI acknowledging the tour stop as instructed, but flagged the mismatch rather than silently inheriting it. Measurements: chapter XVI's real content (the close of the poets'-mistresses triumph, a second garden of streams and dryads, nymphs bathing and making love-play, and a long interior monologue of Poliphilo's doubt and mythic self-comparison) states NO sizes, distances or counts anywhere in its eight pages -- I checked every page for pace/foot/stadium/mile/cubit/palm and found none; this is a lyrical-psychological chapter, not an architectural one. Measurements array is empty for a real reason, not an oversight.*

### Chapter XXII  · Book 1 · 1499 pp. 326–357

*Research: **enumerated**. All 32 pages (326-357) read in translation/en/page_3NN.md. Two findings worth carrying forward. (1) hp.db.woodcut_catalog's page_seq for this chapter's plates runs a consistent ~9-10 pages BEHIND our translation's page numbering -- verified by opening the scans directly (RECIPES/research-a-chapter.md step 2): hp1499_p334.jpg, catalogued at page_seq 334 (#141 'terminal figure with three male heads', #142 'trophy with three heads of Cerberus and serpent'), actually shows the gilt three-headed ithyphallic herm-idol AND the Serapis (lion/dog/wolf, dragon-coiled) image that our translation describes in prose at p.344; hp1499_p341.jpg, catalogued at page_seq 341 (#147 'The Amphitheatre in island of Venus'), carries the printed line 'Area continua per diametro passi.xxxii' -- the Italian for the '32 paces' sentence that is our p.351. Both confirm offset +10. This means plate-to-page joins near a chapter boundary should be checked against the scan, not assumed from page_seq alone -- exactly the kind of thing the woodcut catalogue can get wrong even when a plate exists. (2) Plate #148 ('Ground-plan of fountain of Venus', page_seq 349) is catalogued inside this chapter's page range but, by the same +10 offset (349+10=359), its content is almost certainly the Fountain of Venus precinct that chapter XXIII's text describes starting our p.358 -- the heptagonal plan of seven gemstone columns I viewed at hp1499_p349.jpg matches nothing in chapter XXII's text but matches chapter XXIII's opening exactly. Flagged as xxii-plate-148-fountain-groundplan below and left declined-for-this-chapter; whoever enumerates XXIII should pick it up. (3) Checked every theatre figure found here (Area 32 paces/47.4m, ring 8 paces/11.8m, seats 6 palms/0.44m x 2.5ft/0.74m, top walkway 5ft/1.48m, pergola 1.5 pace/2.22m, crowning cypresses 3 paces/4.44m apart) against DIMENSIONS.md section 4 'The Theatre of Venus' -- all seven agree exactly, no discrepancy. Six new measurements not yet in DIMENSIONS.md are added below (the car's embroidered band, the cornice's clean band, the gallery trough, the plan's bay count, the planted-tier count, and the stair count). (4) The world's amphitheatre (src/scenes/world/cythera.js `_buildAmphitheatre`) and its Cupid-triumph car (src/scenes/world/triumphs.js `_buildCupidTriumph`) are both commented with citations to this exact chapter and this exact translation, and the numbers in those comments match what I independently read -- but per this session's instruction I have not loaded the live running page, so every feature below is `unknown`, not `built`, with the grep evidence named in its note. (5) Godwin 1999 was not consulted; all citations are our own CC0 translation or the 1499 scans.*

### Chapter XXIII  · Book 1 · 1499 pp. 358–368

*Research: **enumerated**. All eleven pages read in full (pp. 358-368: the kneeling before the fountain, the heptagonal fountain's full architecture and gem-lore, the coniunctio program in the columns, the inscription, the curtain of Hymen, the unveiling of Venus, the Adonis/thelygonon/arsenogonon planting and the doves and Peristeria, the Three Graces (Eurydomene/Eurymone/Eurymeduse) and Bacchus-and-Ceres, the six agate steps, Venus's speech assigning eight named attendant nymphs and giving two rings, Cupid's wounding of both lovers, the swoon, the sea-dew healing and re-robing, and Mars's armed arrival and embrace). Checked src/scenes/world/temple.js (_buildFountain, called from cythera.js as this chapter's own fountain, enclosure:true) and src/scenes/world/cythera.js (_buildAmphitheatre, which is chapter XXII's theatre architecture, not this chapter's) by grep for the chapter's names and objects (Synesia, Philedia, Peristeria, Eurydomene, Eurymone, Eurymeduse, Nyctelius/Bacchus, Ceres, Enosina, Monori, Phrontis, Critoa, Adiacorista, Pistinia, Sophrosyne, Edosia, Lycaon, hermaphrodite, dove, socket/infant). Finding: the fountain's ARCHITECTURE (the heptagonal/round kerb, the seven gem columns with their planetary attributions, the crystal cupola and carbuncle, a static Venus primitive standing in the basin with a floating-hair ring, the torn curtain of Hymen as an object, and the fountain's own Greek motto as a plaque) is genuinely built, closely and with real citations to this chapter's own pages -- see temple.js comment block at line ~712 onward. But everything that makes this chapter a SCENE rather than a stage set is missing: no coniunctio figures inside the column shafts, no zodiac carving in the frieze (a plain gold band stands in for it), no doves or Peristeria, no Three Graces (Eurydomene/Eurymone/Eurymeduse -- a DIFFERENT trio of Graces, Aglaia/Euphrosyne/Thalia, exists at an unrelated mainland fountain and is explicitly withheld from this one), no Bacchus-and-Ceres pair (the tour's own prose at tours.json describes their dripping liquor as though built -- 'the water dripped from Bacchus and Ceres beside her' -- but no such geometry exists; this is aspirational tour text, not a built object), no arrow-passing rite with Synesia and Philedia, no wounding, no swoon, no sea-dew healing/re-robing, no eight named attendant nymphs, no rings, and no Mars. A second finding, worth flagging for whoever settles the plate catalogue: catalog plates #149 (p. 363) and #150 (p. 365) fall inside this chapter's page range by page_seq, and I opened both scans (hp1499_p363.jpg, hp1499_p365.jpg) directly -- both show the ALABASTER SEPULCHRE OF ADONIS (the Sardonyx-lidded tomb, the roses medallion reading 'IMPVRA SVAVITAS', nymphs kneeling before it), which is chapter XXIV's own text (our pp. 370-374, already built as _buildAdonis and correctly cited there), not this chapter's curtain-and-fountain unveiling. The plates precede the text they illustrate by several leaves, a known feature of this book's printing, and the catalogue's page_seq should not be read as 'this plate belongs to the chapter with this page range.' I did not find a scan clearly showing #151 ('Poliphilus and Polia at Fountain of Venus with nymphs', also page_seq 365) distinct from the Adonis image on the same page; a reviewer with sqlite access to woodcut_id/link_basis should settle whether #151 is a real second image on that leaf or a duplicate catalog row.*

### Chapter XXVI  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 388–397

*Research: **enumerated**. Read in full: translation/en/page_388.md through page_397.md (our CC0 translation, 1499 pp. 388-397). This is Polia's own narration to the circle of nymphs (Book II): her plague and vow of perpetual chastity to Diana; her admission among Diana's virgins; Poliphilo tracking her down and finding her alone at prayer; her heart freezing 'more freezing than porphyry'; two long love-pleas from Poliphilo (pp. 390-393, one per day, driven off after the first); his death-swoon at her feet (pp. 395-396); and her dragging his corpse into a corner of the temple before fleeing home through Treviso's streets 'as a conscious malefactress' (p. 397). No plague, no dream, no beasts in this chapter -- that is chapter XXVII, next. PLATE-OFFSET FINDING (worth flagging beyond the known trap): woodcut_catalog's page_seq is not the 1499 page directly, despite HPTOTOURPIPELINE.md describing the scan folder as indexed 'by 1499 page' -- in this stretch it is off by a clean +10 (five preliminary leaves not counted in page_seq/page_concordance, which HPTOTOURPIPELINE.md conflates with the translation's own page numbering). Verified against page_concordance (quire/folio) and by reading the actual scans: file hp1499_p386.jpg's text ends '...rachiusi gli somersi occhii allato me se morite' = our p. 396's 'the submerged eyes shut, beside me he died' verbatim, and its woodcut shows Polia standing, reading a book, indifferent, while Poliphilo lies collapsed at her feet -- this is catalog plate #152 ('Polia in temple of Diana; Poliphilus prostrate'), correctly page_seq 386+10=396, NOT excluded as coverage.json's naive page-range math (which used page_seq 387 literally and dropped it as before the chapter) assumed. File hp1499_p387.jpg's text ends '...Qual conscia malefica remeare' = our p. 397's 'as a conscious malefactress to return' verbatim, and its woodcut shows Polia dragging the corpse by the feet into a corner -- this is catalog plate #153 ('Polia drags prostrate Poliphilus from sanctuary'), page_seq 387+10=397. Catalog page_seq for both plates is one leaf short of where the image actually sits (trust the descriptions, not the numbers, per SOURCES.md's existing woodcut-filename warning, now extended to the DB's own page_seq column). Plates #154-156 (page_seq 391-393, so true 1499 pp. 401-403 by the same +10) are confirmed NOT this chapter's: verified by reading the scans at hp1499_p390.jpg (two nude women chained to a burning chariot, dragged by Cupid) and hp1499_p393.jpg (lion and dogs devouring the women, Cupid flying above with a sword, Polia hiding in a thicket) -- this is Polia's nightmare-vision of Cupid's punishment, which chapter XXVII's researcher independently confirmed belongs to their chapter (pp. 399-408), not this one. Grepped src/scenes/world/tombs.js's _buildBookTwo (~L714-823; did not open HPWorldScene.js or Cast.js per the reading-list restriction). It builds one precinct at (44,22): a Temple of Diana (statue, altar, stag, one veiled Polia figure, one Poliphilo figure 'prostrate' near the threshold, two priestesses, a TEMPLVM DIANAE plaque citing plates 152-159 and ch. XXVI), a bed-chamber with the ice/fire-chariot window-vision (later chapters), and the Venus-priestess enthroned (ch. XXXV). No plague/sickbed, no nurse, no dedication-day crowd, no drag-to-the-corner, no polluted corner, no flight through streets, and no Treviso urban fabric (streets/piazza/palace exterior) anywhere in src/scenes/world/ -- grepped the whole folder for street|palazzo|piazza|Treviso and found only the Piazza built for chapter III (unrelated) and this same comment block. None of this is verified live -- statuses below marked 'unknown' where grep found matching code, 'unbuilt' where nothing did. MEASUREMENTS: none. This chapter is pure rhetoric and myth (a love-plea, a death, a flight) with no stated sizes, distances, counts or directions anywhere in pp. 388-397 -- checked against DIMENSIONS.md's units (pace/stadium/foot/cubit) and found nothing to convert; the 'measurements' array below is empty because the chapter states none, not because the pass skipped it.*

### Chapter XXVII  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 398–408

*Research: **enumerated**. Read in full: translation/en/page_398.md through page_408.md (our CC0 translation, 1499 pp. 398-408). This chapter has no woodcut in its own page range, but it is not undepicted: plates 154-156 ('Dream of Polia: Cupid punishes two women' / 'Cupid brandishes sword over kneeling victim' / 'Lion, dog, dragon devour victims; Cupid flies above') sit at 1499 pp. 391-393, which coverage.json's page-range logic assigns to chapter XXVI. But chapter XXVI's own text at those pages (verified pp. 392, 396-397) is Poliphilo's death and Polia's guilty flight from the temple -- it says nothing about a whirlwind, a chariot, or beasts. The vision the three plates depict is only narrated in chapter XXVII's text (pp. 399-408), five to fifteen pages after its own woodcuts. This is a 1499 quire-layout artifact (the block was cut and set before the text it illustrates), not a duplicate telling -- and it means a plate-driven coverage check would credit chapter XXVI with 'covering' a scene its text does not contain, while chapter XXVII -- which spends six pages on it in far more graphic and zoological detail than any three-line caption (six kinds of beast, not 'lion, dog, dragon'; named weapons; hearts torn out) -- shows as plateless and gets skipped. Recommend chapter XXVI's researcher note this cross-reference too. Grepped src/scenes/world/tombs.js (_buildBookTwo, ~L714-823), src/scenes/HPWorldScene.js and src/systems/Cast.js for whirlwind/executioner/nurse/fiery chariot/paliurus/soliferrum/rhomphaea: no matches. The built Book II precinct (_buildBookTwo) covers only the Temple of Diana and the vow (ch. XXV-XXVI, plates 152-153), the bed-chamber's ice-chariot/fire-chariot window vision (ch. XXVI/XXXV, plates 160-165), and the Venus-priestess enthroned (ch. XXXV, plate 163). Nothing from chapter XXVII -- the whirlwind, the punishment-vision, the thorn-thicket, or the nightmare of the two executioners -- exists anywhere in the code. Cast.js already has wolf(), dog(), lion(), eagle() and a generic bird() constructor (grepped, not opened in full) -- most of the beast-feast's cast is already modelled for other scenes and only needs assembling here; kite and vulture have no dedicated model but bird() takes a colour argument.*

*Research: **enumerated**. Read translation/en/page_409.md through page_417.md in full (our CC0 translation). Plates #157-160, catalogued at page_seq 411/412/413/415 (inside this chapter's page range), were opened as scans and all four depict neighbouring-chapter content, not this chapter's text: hp1499_p411.jpg and p412.jpg show Poliphilo dead / revived in Polia's lap (ch. XXIX, the argument printed at the foot of our p.417); hp1499_p413.jpg shows the priestesses driving the lovers out with rods (also ch. XXVII)'). So the plate catalogue's page_seq is offset from this chapter by roughly one chapter forward for #157-159 and one back for #160 — none of the four plates cited against XXVIII in the seeded ledger should be attached to it. Chapter XXVIII, like the vaults of ch. V, is pure text: a nurse's speech, a myth-catalogue, and one extended cautionary tale (the refusing girl, her golden-arrow revenge-marriage, her suicide) that is nowhere drawn and, per this grep, nowhere built. Checked against src/scenes/world/tombs.js (_buildBookTwo, the only Book II geometry in the app) and src/systems/Cast.js was NOT opened (per project instructions, ~197k/large token files are off-limits to this pass) — searched only by grep for character/place names. No hpDiag or live page load was performed this pass (research-only); all 'built'/'partial' status below rests on grep of source, not on loading the running site, per the recipe's caution that a plate number or a nearby structure is a weak hint, not proof.*

### Chapter XXIX  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 418–427

*Research: **enumerated**. Read translation/en/page_418.md through page_427.md in full (all ten pages, plus the ready-made per-page Notes). Chapter XXIX is Polia's own narration: the flame of Love finally kindles in her (pp.418-419, against a catalogue of love's metamorphosed victims); she runs to the Temple of Diana, finds Poliphilo's corpse, laments over it like Laodamia, and revives him by touch and tears (pp.420-422); Diana's priestesses beat the lovers apart and banish Polia (pp.423-424); the two flee to the city (Treviso), exchange betrothal vows and part; Polia goes home transformed -- Diana's image gone from her mind, Poliphilo's installed -- and makes him love-tokens (pp.424-425); that night she sees a vision of Diana's ice-chariot routed by Venus's fire-chariot through her bed-chamber window (pp.425-426); she resolves to go to Venus's temple, confesses her whole cruelty to the priestess, and vows herself to Venus and to Poliphilo, whereupon the priestess calls him forward -- the exact seam into Book I's temple-rite (p.427). PLATE-OFFSET TRAP CONFIRMED, and it runs in BOTH directions across this chapter's boundaries: hp.db.woodcut_catalog's page_seq for the plates that actually illustrate chapter XXIX's own text (#157-160, catalogued at page_seq 411,412,413,415) is offset about -10 pages from the translation page the scene occurs on, so coverage_seed.py's naive page-range match currently files them under chapter XXVIII (pp.409-417) instead -- I opened the facsimile scans (hp1499_p411/412/413/415.jpg) and read the Italian directly against our translation to confirm: p411's image + caption text matches our p.420-421 (Polia's lament and the Argia simile just before the pulse revives); p412 matches our p.422 almost word for word ('Polia Signora mia dolce, perche cusi atorto me fai' = 'Polia, my sweet Lady, why so wrongfully dost thou make me suffer?'), including the Hermetic Caduceus line; p413 matches our p.423 (Medusa/Atalanta/Proetides fears, the beating); p415 matches our p.425 (the crimson-heart/hair-chaplet passage running straight into the ice-chariot vision). Conversely, plates #161-163 (page_seq 419,419,425), which coverage_seed.py's page-range match currently (wrongly) attaches to chapter XXIX because 419 and 425 fall inside its nominal 418-427 span, do NOT belong here: I opened hp1499_p419.jpg and hp1499_p425.jpg and their text is Poliphilo's petition to the priestess ('che ambi dui uno solo ligamine... inuinculare facesse') and the couple already kissing before her ('hora hauendo sol paceamente esso basiato') -- both belong to chapter XXX (pp.428-431), which is exactly what the tours.json 'Before the Priestess' note (chapter XXX-XXXI) already independently describes for woodcuts 161-163. Net effect: chapter XXIX's real plates are 157, 158, 159, 160 -- none of which the ledger currently lists for it. Whoever next refreshes chapter XXVIII or XXX should carry this correction; I did not touch either chapter's file. Cross-checked the world against src/scenes/world/tombs.js _buildBookTwo (read directly, not HPWorldScene.js/Cast.js) and src/data/tours.json's three 'book_two' stops for chapters XXVI/XXVII/XXIX; did not load the running page, so nothing below is marked built.*

### Chapter XXX  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 428–431

*Research: **enumerated**. Read pp. 428–431 in full (translation/en/page_428.md–page_431.md, our CC0 translation, plus the per-page notes). Chapter XXX is Poliphilo's spoken plea to the priestess of Venus that she bind him and Polia as one, and Polia's own account of watching him plead, ending mid-sentence as she is about to interrupt. IMPORTANT CORRECTION to the premise this chapter was assigned under ('no plates'): that premise comes from woodcut_catalog.page_seq falling outside this chapter's derived page range, and it is wrong. woodcut_catalog's page_seq for this stretch of the book runs a consistent 10 pages BEHIND the true 1499 page — confirmed by opening the scans directly and matching their printed Italian text against our translation: the scan filed as hp1499_p415.jpg opens 'cum gli mei longissimi capilli evulsi...', which is verbatim our translation page 425 ('with my longest hairs, plucked...'), not page 415; the scan hp1499_p419.jpg's printed text is verbatim our page 429; hp1499_p421.jpg's is verbatim our page 431; hp1499_p425.jpg's is verbatim our page 435. So: catalog #161 (nominal page_seq 419, 'Polia kneels before Venus priestess; Poliphilus beside') is really at true page 429 — Poliphilo standing, Polia kneeling before the enthroned priestess in a tetrastyle hall with a lit altar and a barred window — squarely inside chapter XXX, illustrating the very opening of his plea. Catalog #162 (also nominal page_seq 419 — the catalogue lists two different plates at the identical page_seq, itself a red flag) does NOT match the single image actually present at true page 429 ('Polia kneels...' is a one-image page); its real content — two couples kneeling before a priestess and her nymphs at a pedimented temple doorway, with a small dog — is the woodcut on the scan filed hp1499_p421.jpg, true page 431, this chapter's own last page. So XXX has two genuine plates, not zero, and neither is presently attached to it in the ledger's plate derivation. Cross-checked against src/scenes/world/tombs.js: the only Book II geometry at a Venus-priestess tribunal (_buildBookTwo, ~L805–823) is posed and labelled for the KISS (chapter XXXI's climax, plate #163 correctly identified — see XXXI.json), not for Poliphilo's plea or for the temple-door scene; I have not loaded the live site this session, so even that is recorded as unknown, not built. Measurements: none stated in this chapter — pp. 428–431 are entirely dialogue, interior monologue and mythological simile; no pace, foot, cubit, stadium or count is given anywhere in the text.*

### Chapter XXXI  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 432–435

*Research: **enumerated**. Read pp. 432–435 in full (translation/en/page_432.md–page_435.md, our CC0 translation, plus the per-page notes). Chapter XXXI is Polia's answering declaration of love — a long speech reversing every refusal of chs. XXV–XXIX — capped by the betrothal kiss (the arra) and the priestess's ruling that she need not intervene because Love has already joined them. CORRECTION to the premise this chapter was assigned under (that it has two plates, #164 and #165): it does not. The same page_seq offset documented for chapter XXX (woodcut_catalog.page_seq runs 10 pages behind the true 1499 page in this stretch of the book) means #164 (nominal page_seq 433) and #165 (nominal page_seq 435) are NOT inside this chapter at all. Confirmed by reading the scans directly and matching their printed Italian text: hp1499_p433.jpg's text is verbatim our translation's page 443 ('gloriosa morte, miseramente uiuendo...' = 'glorious death, miserably living...'), which is chapter XXXII — Poliphilo's own retrospective lament while writing his first letter, not anything in XXXI. hp1499_p435.jpg's text is verbatim our page 445, the opening of chapter XXXIII. Both plates' true subjects (Poliphilus writing at a desk; Polia reading the letter in her bed-chamber) belong with the tour's own 'Poliphilo's Telling: the Love-Letters' stop (chs. XXXII–XXXIII) — whose folio citation in src/data/tours.json ('woodcuts 164–165, folios 433–435') is itself off by the same 10 pages and should read approximately folios 443/445. The plate that DOES genuinely belong to XXXI is catalog #163 ('Priestess enthroned; lovers kissing in her presence', nominal page_seq 425): its true page is 435 (425+10), confirmed the same way — the scan hp1499_p425.jpg's printed text below the image is verbatim our translation's page 435, the chapter's closing scene. So chapter XXXI has exactly one real plate, and it is the chapter's own climax. Measurements: none stated — pp. 432–435 are Polia's declaration, a catalogue of mythological exempla, and the kiss; no pace, foot, cubit, stadium or count appears anywhere in the text.*

### Chapter XXXII  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 436–443

*Research: **enumerated**. Read translation/en/page_436.md through page_443.md in full, both the translated text and every page's Notes block. Chapter XXXII is Poliphilo's own narration, delivered aloud to the enthroned Priestess of Venus with Polia present (the frame the priestess opened in ch. XXXI, p. 435): he praises perseverance as the book's moral, then tells his side of falling in love -- first sight of Polia at a festival in the Temple of Diana, his coup de foudre, his vow of total devotion ('no other image...affixable...but hers'), the pain of her departure (Laodamia/Ariadne/Io similes), a spiral into cursing her and a repentance of the curse, and his final resolve at p. 443 to write her a letter. Its own page range (436-443) has NO catalogued plate in hp.db.woodcut_catalog and the site's src/images/woodcuts/ has nothing for it either -- the 'plateless chapter' framing holds for THIS page range. BUT: hp.db.woodcut_catalog's page_seq for catalog_number 164 ('Poliphilus writing at carved desk') is recorded as 433 and the ledger's seeder therefore files it under chapter XXXI (pp. 432-435). I opened the scan directly (site/images/woodcuts_1499/hp1499_p433.jpg) and its printed text is NOT p. 433's content -- it is our translation's p. 443 verbatim ('...Hei Poliphile, contra il tuo bene...Herostrato...Et la ritonda Pila apta di rotarse...' = 'Hey, Poliphilo, against thy good...Herostratus...the round Ball apt to roll'). So the scan/catalog page_seq in this stretch of Book II runs a consistent ~10 pages BEHIND the true 1499/our-translation page number (confirmed again independently for ch. XXXIII/XXXV below). Plate 164 therefore belongs to CHAPTER XXXII, at its own closing page (443, the decision to write), not to XXXI. XXXII is not plateless once the offset is corrected -- it has exactly one plate, and it was hiding under the wrong chapter. Godwin 1999 not consulted. No new measurements: the chapter is pure interior monologue and classical simile, no stated sizes, counts, or distances (see measurements: []).*

### Chapter XXXIII  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 444–448

*Research: **enumerated**. Read translation/en/page_444.md through page_448.md in full (text + Notes). Chapter XXXIII is entirely Poliphilo's two courtly love-letters to Polia, framed by two short bridging paragraphs (p. 444 sending the first, p. 446-447 sending the second after the first fails) and closing with the argument of chapter XXXIV (p. 448, which is not this chapter's content and is left for whoever researches XXXIV). IMPORTANT CORRECTION to the ledger's current plates[] for this chapter: hp.db.woodcut_catalog lists catalog_numbers 166-168 (page_seq 447, 448, 448; 'Poliphilus before Venus in clouds; Cupid listens', 'Cupid with bust of Polia and arrow', 'Cupid shoots arrow at bust of Polia') as falling in this chapter's page range by naive page-number matching. They do NOT belong here. I opened both scans directly: site/images/woodcuts_1499/hp1499_p447.jpg's printed text is our translation's p. 457 verbatim ('Audite benignamente le mie lamentabile querimonie... quella uera & diua effigie di Polia' = 'Having benignly heard my lamentable complaints... that true and divine effigy of Polia'), and hp1499_p448.jpg's is p. 458's ('Et poscia alla genitrice... Nel delicato pecto della ostensa imagine... sagitta'). Both are chapter XXXV (the vision at Venus's throne, where Cupid shoots Polia's effigy) -- SOURCES.md's own misfiled-woodcuts table already half-flagged this for plate #166 ('now shown at ch. XXXV') but the ledger's page-range seeding still pulls all three into XXXIII. The scan/catalog page_seq in this whole stretch of Book II runs a consistent ~10 pages behind the true 1499/our-translation page (433->443, 435/436->445/446, 447->457, 448->458 -- checked four independent points). So: chapter XXXIII, on its own real pages 444-448, has ONE plate, not three -- see xxxiii-letter-delivery-bedchamber below (catalog #165, recorded page_seq 435, true page 446) -- and it is currently misfiled under chapter XXXI by the same offset. Whoever next runs coverage_seed.py on this chapter should expect its derived plates[] to say 166-168 and should override that; the true single plate is #165. Godwin 1999 not consulted. No measurements stated anywhere in these five pages -- the whole chapter is direct address, no distances, sizes, or counts (see measurements: []).*

### Chapter XXXIV  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 449–455

*Research: **enumerated**. Chapter XXXIV has NO PLATE of its own -- hp.db.woodcut_catalog returns zero rows for page_seq 449-455 (woodcut 165 is p. 435, chapter XXXIII; nothing appears again until 166 at p. 447, also XXXIII). It is Poliphilo's own narration of the courtship's failure and his death: his third and final letter to Polia (pp. 449-451, 'the more I love thee, the more I lapidise thee'), his vain devotions to Cupid and exhaustive search of Treviso's streets and porticoes for her (pp. 451-452), finding her alone in the Sacramentary Temple and collapsing dead at her feet while she watches unmoved (pp. 453-454), and her dawn revival of him (p. 455) -- the same death-and-revival Polia narrated from her own side in chapters XXVI and XXIX, now from his. No measured distances, paces or physical dimensions are stated anywhere in the chapter; the only countable things are narrative (the THIRD letter of three). Per Ted's 2026-09-17 direction that Book II is built as a real second place, the chapter's told city -- Polia's 'superb palace', the streets and porticoes Poliphilo ransacks -- is now buildable geometry, not narration to wave at. Some events (the temple death, the dawn revival) are the same moment the world already stages for chapter XXVI/XXIX at the Book II precinct (src/scenes/world/tombs.js _buildBookTwo, Temple of Diana block, ~line 736) -- graded 'unknown' here, not 'built', because this session did not load the live page, and because that build represents Polia's telling, not this re-telling's specific beats (the lion-pounce, the liquefying to wax).*

### Chapter XXXV  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 456–460

*Research: **enumerated**. Chapter XXXV has NO PLATE of its own -- hp.db.woodcut_catalog returns zero rows for page_seq 456-460. The nearest plates (166-168) fall at pages 447-448, inside chapter XXXIII's text as translated (translation/en/page_447.md, page_448.md), TWO PAGES BEFORE chapter XXXIV even opens -- so the catalogue's page_seq for these three plates does not line up with the events they depict (Venus in the clouds, Cupid with Polia's bust, Cupid shooting the bust), which are narrated only here in XXXV, pp. 456-458. This is a genuine mismatch worth a ticket: either the catalogue's page_seq is off for #166-168, or the 1499's plates were set ahead of the text they illustrate (a known period layout habit). This pass treats the plates as belonging to this chapter's events on content grounds, per hp.db's own descriptions, while leaving the numeric page_seq discrepancy on record. The chapter itself is Poliphilo's near-death vision: his soul, freed at his death (the close of ch. XXXIV), rises to Venus enthroned in the clouds, complains against Cupid, watches Cupid strike Polia's divine effigy with the golden arrow and win her yielding, is shown a beatific vision of Polia's celestial beauty, hears Venus's world-softening voice, and returns to his body. This chapter is also where the world's own tour text for chapter XXXV is attached -- to 'quinta_essentia' (src/scenes/world/constants.js line 57), which is a pre-existing BOOK I station, 'The Obelisk of the Trinity' (folio 119). No ground of its own has been modelled for this chapter's heavenly court; the note is attached to unrelated Book I geometry. Separately, tombs.js's built Venus-priestess-enthroned scene (_buildBookTwo, ~line 828) is code-commented 'sub: ENTHRONED . CH. XXXV', but its plate (163, p. 425) and its content (a human priestess on earth, the lovers kissing before her) actually belongs to chapters XXX-XXXI, not this chapter's heavenly throne (Venus in the clouds, not a priestess on earth). That mislabel is worth a ticket of its own: a code comment naming this chapter proves someone looked, not that this chapter's content exists. No measured distances, paces or physical dimensions are stated anywhere in the chapter; the only countable things are narrative (three presences at the throne; six gods named as susceptible to Venus's voice; three zodiacal figures named as banished from it).*

### Chapter XXXVIII  · Book 2 · 1499 pp. 465–465
